description: We build "Geçit Hava" for the 2026 challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!": historical probability for a chosen place and day from 1991-2026 NASA POWER/MERRA-2 daily data, plus trend analysis with OLS slope, 95% CI and the Mann-Kendall test. Shipped as a single-file offline web app. Team covers data, analysis, frontend, testing. Looking for: Earth Science knowledge, statistics/Python or frontend skills, and someone for slides or a 45-second demo video.

Annual mean temperature is significant in all 258 cells, with a median of +0.62 °C per decade; precipitation is significant in only 48 of 258. details:
Geçit Hava is a trend map, not a forecast. It shows where Türkiye's climate is actually changing and whether that change is statistically real.

What it does: we pull NASA POWER/MERRA-2 monthly data (1991–2025) for 258 land grid cells inside Türkiye, for six variables (mean, max and min temperature, precipitation, wind speed, relative humidity). For every calendar month we compute the decadal slope, so the seasonal cycle is excluded by construction. The map colours each cell by change per decade; cells that fail significance are faded and hatched — a colour without evidence would be a false claim. Clicking a cell shows its 35-year series, the OLS slope, a 95% confidence interval, the t-test p-value and the Mann-Kendall p-value, plus a badge that says whether the two tests agree.

Impact: annual mean temperature is significant in all 258 cells (median +0.62 °C per decade, up to +0.82 °C south of Ankara), while precipitation is significant in only 48 — an honest map tells you where not to claim change. Farmers, water managers, municipalities and researchers can check any region in seconds, and the whole map exports to CSV.

Tools: Node.js data pipeline, vanilla JavaScript and SVG for the visualisation, no server, no framework. Statistics implemented from first principles (OLS with Student-t intervals, tie-corrected Mann-Kendall, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR).

Creativity: the interface treats uncertainty as a first-class visual element, and the tool is fully offline in a single HTML file, so it works on a laptop in the field.
